title: Earn, save, give
hookLine: Wesley's sermon on money: gain all you can honestly, save all you can, give all you can

cards: A paycheck lands on a Friday. Before a cent of it is spent, its owner has already sorted it: rent, the car, groceries, that thing in the online cart, and maybe, if anything is left, something for somebody else.

John Wesley, the preacher whose followers became the Methodists, wrote a sermon about exactly that moment, called The Use of Money. Preachers are sometimes expected to treat money as a danger to keep at arm's length.
Wesley didn't. He told his listeners to go out and earn.

teach.b: Wesley's sermon gives money three rules, in order. First, gain all you can, but honestly, and with limits: not by work that wrecks your own health, not by hurting your neighbor, their body, their business or their soul.
Earning, for Wesley, was part of faithfulness, as long as nobody paid for it with harm.
Second, save all you can. And here's the surprise: by save, Wesley didn't mean stockpile. He meant cut the waste.
Don't throw money at showing off, at things bought to be admired, at feeding every craving. Saving kept money free for something better. Third, give all you can.

That's where the first two were heading the whole time. In his telling, someone who earns hard and saves hard but stops there has missed the point and only built a bigger pile. Wesley wasn't inventing this.
Paul tells a reformed thief in Ephesians to work with his hands, and gives the reason: "that he may have to give to him that needeth." Earning, there, points outward from the start.

teach.h: THE LOVE OF MONEY, NOT MONEY.
teach.b: Paul also warns Timothy that "the love of money is the root of all evil." Notice the word: the love of it, not the money itself. Wesley's three rules are one way of keeping the money and losing the love.
Earn so you have something. Save so it isn't wasted. Give, because that was what it was for.

how: Methodists and other Christians still teach from Wesley's sermon The Use of Money; churches often use it in teaching on stewardship, budgeting and giving.

games.q: Wesley's money rules — tap the pairs.
p: where the first two were heading

s: Wesley told Christians to keep money at arm's length
his first rule was gain all you can, as long as it was honest and harmed no one.
by save, Wesley meant build up a big pile
he meant cut the waste: spending on showing off and craving. saving kept money free to give.
Paul tells a reformed thief to work so he can give
Ephesians 4:28: "that he may have to give to him that needeth."

games.q: you're one of Wesley's listeners. you've earned well and saved hard, and the account is growing. what does the sermon say comes next?
games.why: Wesley's third rule is give all you can. in his telling, earning and saving without giving misses the point of both.

practice: Think back over the last week of spending and find one small thing you didn't really need, a delivery fee, a second coffee, an impulse buy: that amount is saved money in Wesley's sense, waste you could cut.
Now ask where it could go instead, a neighbor, a food bank, a friend who's short this month, a cause you already trust. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart.

wordCard.voice: Earn. In Wesley's sermon, the first of three rules for money: gain all you can, honestly, without harm, so that you have something to save and to give.

carryVoice: Your line: give all you can. The pile was never the point. See you tomorrow.
